findings.headline: SEND placement costs have only limited assurance control despite structural demand growth
findings.detail: Sandwell faces growing demand for SEND placements driven by population growth and earlier diagnosis of autism and other conditions. A transformation partner was engaged in January 2026 and a permanent SEND and Inclusion Service Director starts in August. However, internal audit assigned only limited assurance to the council's controls over placement cost management in this structurally growing service area.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on controls for a high-cost, structurally growing service signals the council may struggle to contain costs; this exposes the MTFS to pressure and creates audit risk
findings.figures: No specific placement cost or demand growth figures disclosed
findings.quote: Internal Audit review 2025/26 – SEND placement costs – Limited assurance

findings.headline: Housing regulator issued C3 rating in October 2024; improvement underway but electrical safety given limited assurance
findings.detail: The Regulator for Social Housing rated Sandwell C3 (service requiring regulatory attention) in October 2024. The council is delivering a Housing Improvement and Transformation Plan with Phase 2 launching Q2 2026, and has established a CEO-led Housing Oversight Board. However, internal audit found only limited assurance on electrical installation condition reporting (EICR) compliance.
findings.matters: A C3 rating signals the social housing regulator identified material compliance or governance failures; combined with limited assurance on safety compliance, it indicates risk in a major council asset and service domain
findings.figures: C3 rating issued October 2024
findings.quote: Risk reflects the C3 regulatory judgement issued by the Regulator for Social Housing in October 2024 and progress made on delivery of the Housing Improvement and Transformation Plan

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspend on High Needs Block poses material General Fund and MTFS risk
findings.detail: Sandwell faces a forecast overspend on the DSG High Needs Block, reflecting national SEND demand pressures. The register explicitly flags that this must be mitigated in the medium term to prevent cascade to the General Fund and destabilisation of the MTFS. Transformation planning is underway, and a permanent SEND Director starts in August, but specific savings proposals and timelines for mitigation are still being developed.
findings.matters: A lender funding a council needs to know schools funding pressures won't cascade to core services and that the council has credible plans to contain a structurally growing cost area
findings.figures: No specific DSG overspend quantum is disclosed
findings.quote: The Council will need to put in place a DSG mitigation plan to ensure that the forecast overspend for the High Needs Block can be mitigated in the medium-term, so that there is no impact on the General Fund, which could de-stabilise the MTFS

findings.headline: Inconsistent compliance with governance frameworks across services; variability in adherence to policies and procedures
findings.detail: Assurance activity has identified variability in adherence to internal governance requirements across services, including compliance with policies, procedures and audit recommendations. This is identified as a significant governance issue requiring continued focus to ensure governance standards are applied consistently across the organisation.
findings.matters: Inconsistent governance enforcement across a council indicates weak central control and oversight. This increases the risk that material issues in individual services go undetected or unmanaged until they become serious problems.
findings.figures: None specified; identified through assurance activity
findings.quote: Assurance activity has identified variability in adherence to internal governance requirements across services, including compliance with policiesand its ongoing implementation will be reviewed during 2026/27, alongside a refreshed self‑assessment.

findings.headline: Council faces ongoing financial pressures and emerging funding gaps from 2027/28; relying on Corporate Transformation Programme to deliver savings
findings.detail: Council acknowledges continued financial pressures and increasing reliance on transformation activity to deliver sustainable savings. Significant governance issue identified around delivery of Corporate Transformation Programme, with emerging funding gaps expected from 2027/28. Programme governance structures were revised in May 2025 to strengthen prioritisation and accountability. No savings figures disclosed.
findings.matters: A council dependent on transformation savings to manage gaps from 2027/28 onwards faces execution risk. If savings do not materialise or are delayed, the council will face a budget crisis. The need to strengthen programme governance in May 2025 suggests prior delivery challenges.
findings.figures: Emerging funding gaps from 2027/28; Corporate Transformation Programme structures revised May 2025; specific savings targets not disclosed
findings.quote: The Council faces ongoing financial pressures, with increasing reliance on transformation activity to deliver sustainable savings... in response to emerging funding gaps from 2027/28, supporting the Council's long‑term financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing found serious failings in Safety and Quality Consumer Standard; large contract overspends on major housing capital projects
findings.detail: In October 2024, regulator published judgement finding serious failings in housing service delivery against Safety and Quality Consumer Standard. Council has identified out-of-date stock condition surveys and building safety compliance issues from self-referral. Multiple major capital housing projects experienced delays and large contract overspends. Housing Improvement Programme now in place with structured monitoring.
findings.matters: Regulatory intervention in social housing is rare and serious. Capital project overspends on housing indicate cost control failures. Combined with asset condition survey gaps, this suggests governance and project management weaknesses in a major asset class.
findings.figures: October 2024 regulatory judgement; multiple major capital projects with delays and large overspends (amounts not specified); out-of-date stock surveys; building safety compliance checks outstanding
findings.quote: In October 2024 the Regulator of Social Housing published a Regulatory Judgement in relation to the recently adopted Consumer Standards... The regulator reached a conclusion that there were serious failings in delivering the outcome of the Safety and Quality Consumer Standard, and that significant improvement was needed. There were also delays and large contract overspends on several major capital housing projects.

findings.headline: External audit unable to form opinions on Council accounts for three consecutive years; rebuilding assurance expected to take until 2028
findings.detail: 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts both received disclaimer opinions under backstop deadline legislation. 2024/25 audit also resulted in disclaimer, mainly because opening balances could not be assured due to insufficient 2023/24 audit work. Council plans retrospective audit work after 2025/26 to rebuild historical assurance, with full assurance not expected until 2028.
findings.matters: Inability to gain external audit assurance on three years of accounts is a major weakness. Statutory backstop deadlines prevented full audits, but the gap remains a fundamental governance and accountability gap. Full restoration is 2+ years away.
findings.figures: Disclaimer opinions: 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25; backstop deadline for 2025/26 is 31 January 2027; aim to publish by 30 November 2026; full assurance target 2028
findings.quote: Grant Thornton's audit opinions were issued with a disclaimer of opinion. Effectively this means that the auditor was not able to gain the assurance necessary to give an unmodified opinion by the backstop date... A disclaimer of opinion was once again issued by the external auditor, however, mainly due to not being able to gain assurance over opening balances due to insufficient audit work having taken place in relation to the 2023/24 accounts.

findings.headline: Six limited assurance audit reports issued in 2025/26, including on SEND placement costs and Children's Trust financial outturn
findings.detail: Internal audit issued six limited assurance ratings across key areas: SEND Placement Costs, Sandwell Children's Trust Financial Outturn 2024/25, Procurement and Contract Compliance, Payroll, Boscobel Tenant Management Organisation, and Housing Improvement Electrical Safety Inspections. Of 25 total reviews completed, only 3 achieved substantial assurance.
findings.matters: Limited assurance indicates material internal control weaknesses that require management attention. The concentration in high-risk areas (SEND spending, children's services, payroll, procurement) signals systemic control issues rather than isolated problems.
findings.figures: 6 limited assurance reports out of 25 total reviews (24% of audits with limited assurance); breakdown: 3 substantial, 16 reasonable, 6 limited, 0 none
findings.quote: They also noted that they had issued six limited assurance reports during the year, in the following areas: SEND Placement Costs, Sandwell Children's Trust Financial Outturn 2024/25, Procurement and Contract Compliance, Payroll, Boscobel Tenant Management Organisation, Housing Improvement Electrical Safety Inspections

findings.headline: Sandwell Children's Trust has accumulated deficits requiring additional funding to reach breakeven by 2027/28
findings.detail: The Trust, which delivers children's social care, has spent beyond its annual allocation each year. Council has agreed a three-year contract with additional sums in each year to offset the cumulative deficit by 2027/28. The Trust must manage within the funded envelope and offset any annual overspends with underspends in other years within the three-year period.
findings.matters: An arm's-length delivery vehicle essential to statutory services is dependent on additional Council funding to balance. If the Trust continues to overspend, it signals control and cost management issues that the Council cannot easily exit.
findings.figures: Three-year contract from 2025/26 with additional sums each year to offset cumulative deficit by 2027/28
findings.quote: The Children's Trust had accumulated financial deficits through increased expenditure beyond that allocated through the annual contract sum process. In response, a three‑year contact sum was agreed from 2025/26, along with an additional sum in each of the three years in order to offset the cumulative deficit by 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Grant Thornton Audit Plan to year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Uncertainty over whether group financial statements are required, creating potential for unrecorded consolidations
findings.detail: Management has not yet determined whether the authority is required to prepare group financial statements. The auditors have requested a formal accounting paper setting out management's consideration of factors that may require group accounts. This suggests the scope of consolidation may be unclear.
findings.matters: If the authority has material subsidiaries, joint ventures or associates that should be consolidated but are not, the reported financial position would be incomplete. This is a gap in financial reporting governance.
findings.figures: Group materiality set at £19.375m if group accounts are prepared
findings.quote: Management is yet to determine whether the Authority is required to prepare group financial statements. We have requested a formal accounting paper from management setting out their consideration of factors that may require the preparation of group accounts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Grant Thornton Audit Plan to year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Multiple unresolved value-for-money risk areas requiring further investigation: Children's Trust, DSG deficit, housing and Oracle systems
findings.detail: Beyond the confirmed significant weakness on accounts production, auditors have identified key lines of enquiry in several high-risk areas: Sandwell Children's Trust (a separate organisation), a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, housing arrangements, the Oracle financial system, and the Alfred Gunn Project. These will be investigated during the audit.
findings.matters: Multiple concurrent risk areas suggest either emerging problems or historical issues not yet resolved. DSG deficits, trust governance, and IT system control weaknesses can each trigger further audit findings or financial deterioration.
findings.figures: Not specified in plan; to be determined during audit procedures
findings.quote: We have also identified key lines of enquiry in a number of areas that we will look to explore covering arrangements regarding Sandwell Children's Trust, Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, housing, Oracle, and the Alfred Gunn Project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Grant Thornton Audit Plan to year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Bank reconciliations not being performed regularly in a timely manner, creating risk of misstated cash balances
findings.detail: The auditors have identified that the authority is not performing regular bank reconciliations in a timely manner. There is a risk that the cash and overdraft balances reported in the balance sheet could be misstated if the year-end reconciliation is done after the draft financial statements are produced, as appears to be current practice.
findings.matters: Bank reconciliation is a fundamental internal control. If not performed promptly, errors in cash balances—a material asset—go undetected. This is especially concerning given the prior-year disclaimer, as cash is one area where assurance must be rebuilt.
findings.figures: Planning materiality £19.3m; clearly trivial threshold £0.965m
findings.quote: The Authority has not been performing regular bank reconciliations in a timely manner. There is a risk that the cash and overdraft balances on the Authority's Balance Sheet could be misstated in the draft financial statements if the year-end bank reconciliation process takes place after the financial statements have been produced.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Grant Thornton Audit Plan to year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Significant weakness identified for third consecutive year: authority failing to draft and publish accounts on time
findings.detail: The auditors have identified a significant weakness in the authority's arrangements for preparing accurate financial statements in a timely manner. This is the same issue raised in both 2023/24 and 2024/25 Auditor's Annual Reports, meaning the council failed to meet statutory deadlines in both prior years and the prior-year recommendation was not implemented.
findings.matters: Failure to produce auditable accounts on time creates cascading delays in audit completion, prevents public scrutiny of the council's finances, and when repeated over years indicates a systemic weakness in finance function capability or resourcing.
findings.figures: Repeated finding across 2023/24 and 2024/25; backstop deadline for 2025/26 accounts is 31 January 2027
findings.quote: In both our 2023/24 and 2024/25 Auditor's Annual Reports, we concluded that the Authority failed to draft and publish its annual statement of accounts on a timely basis. We issued a key recommendation requiring the Authority to make significant improvements to its arrangements for preparing accurate financial statements in a timely manner to support an efficient audit process.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: Grant Thornton Audit Plan to year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Prior year audit disclaimer due to backstop date, with limited assurance recovery planned for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 audit because audit work was not completed before the legal backstop date. For 2025/26, the auditors will have limited assurance over opening balances and no assurance over closing reserves balances due to the uncertainty over opening amounts. They are working with the council to rebuild assurance over time, with an internal target of 30 November 2026.
findings.matters: A disclaimer means the auditor could not form an opinion on whether the financial statements are true and fair. Lenders and the council's own finance director cannot be confident in the reported financial position.
findings.figures: Prior year gross operating costs £1,072m (materiality set at £19.3m for 2025/26, up from £16.5m)
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the backstop. As a result, we anticipate that for 2025/26: we will have limited assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26; no assurance over the closing reserves balance, due to the uncertainty over their opening amount.

findings.headline: Planned borrowing requirement of £46.5m only drawn at 46%, with £25m less debt than budgeted
findings.detail: Borrowing was budgeted at £46.522m but actual draw was only £21.485m (46% utilisation), a variance of £25.037m underdraw. This substantial gap mirrors the capital programme underspend and suggests either projects did not progress as planned or capital financing needs were materially overestimated.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor planned versus actual borrowing to assess debt forecasting accuracy and capital strategy credibility; a £25m variance between budgeted and actual borrowing is material to leverage ratios, debt trajectory projections, and confidence in the council's financial planning process.
findings.figures: Budgeted borrowing £46.522m, actual £21.485m, variance £25.037m (54% underdraw)

findings.headline: Overall HRA capital programme underspent by £30.2m (33% variance), with only 67% of £92.6m budget executed
findings.detail: The total HRA capital programme budgeted at £92.552m achieved only £62.330m in actual expenditure, a variance of £30.222m underspent. This material shortfall is spread across both New Build and Investment categories, indicating either broad forecasting inaccuracy or programme-wide delivery challenges.
findings.matters: Large-scale underspend raises questions about forecasting reliability and capital delivery capability; for a lender assessing council financial credibility, this variance suggests either overestimated capital ambitions or execution obstacles that affect both operational risk and the reliability of the council's forward financial projections.
findings.figures: Total budgeted £92.552m, actual £62.330m, variance £30.222m underspent

findings.headline: Major Projects capital category underspent by £19.5m, executing at only 39% of the £31.9m budget
findings.detail: Within the Investment category, Major Projects were budgeted at £31.891m but only £12.435m was spent (39% execution), creating a variance of £19.457m. This is the single largest underspend in the capital programme and indicates material delays or non-execution of major capital schemes.
findings.matters: Lenders assess council capital delivery capability as an indicator of operational effectiveness and resilience; Major Projects underperformance at this scale suggests either overambitious forecasting or significant delivery obstacles that could affect housing stock development, future service capacity, and the council's ability to execute its capital strategy.
findings.figures: Major Projects: budgeted £31.891m, actual £12.435m (39% execution, £19.457m underspend)

findings.headline: Housing directorate spent only £5.77m of £13.19m budget (44%), indicating systemic underperformance across the division
findings.detail: Beyond Disabled Facilities Grants, the wider Housing directorate spent only 44% of its £13.19m budget. Empty Properties redevelopment spent just £45k of £679k, and other schemes show similar delays. This is half the overall capital programme delivery rate.
findings.matters: Directorate-level underspending indicates either demand changes, staffing constraints, or procurement delays across multiple housing schemes. For lenders, this signals broader project management weaknesses.
findings.figures: Housing total budget £13,185k, spent £5,767k (44%), slippage £7,418k

findings.headline: Approved prudential borrowing only 49% deployed, leaving £12.2m of £24.1m unused despite formal authorization
findings.detail: The council authorized £24,097k of prudential borrowing for 2025/26 but spent only £11,898k (49%), with £12,199k underspent. Although £12m is expected to slip to 2026/27, this indicates capital projects are not progressing as scheduled despite formal approval.
findings.matters: Low utilization of approved prudential borrowing suggests projects are delayed despite authorization, raising questions about delivery capacity and whether the council's debt assumptions remain realistic.
findings.figures: Approved borrowing £24,097k, spent £11,898k (49%), variance £12,199k, slippage £12,007k

findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grants delivered only £4.96m of £11.64m budget (43%), a statutory service significantly underspent
findings.detail: This statutory housing support service spent only 43% of its budget, with £6.68m slipping into future years. This is less than half the overall capital programme delivery rate of 71%, and Disabled Facilities Grants typically has strong take-up and dedicated funding.
findings.matters: Statutory service underspend suggests staffing capacity or process delays in a core housing function. For lenders, this indicates potential management weaknesses in delivering mandatory services.
findings.figures: Budgeted £11,639k, spent £4,961k (43%), slippage £6,678k
findings.quote: Disabled Facilities Grants 11,639 11,639 4,961 (6,678) 6,678 -

findings.headline: King George V Primary School £250k scheme involves Grade II listed building currently in disrepair, with execution risk dependent on heritage approval.
findings.detail: The council proposes to restore a listed former site manager's house to create nursery provision. The building has been vacant and is now in poor condition. Cabinet approval is explicitly limited: 'No works should proceed unless and until officers have confirmed the full property, planning and heritage position and secured any necessary permissions or consents.' Cost overruns and delays are possible given listed status and current condition.
findings.matters: Listed building restoration carries execution risk. Scope uncertainty, heritage constraints, and structural unknowns can drive cost overruns or delay delivery. The £250k allocation may be insufficient if condition assessments reveal additional works needed.
findings.figures: £250k council allocation (£200k School Condition Allocation + £50k High Needs Capital Allocation); £150k DfE capital grant also involved; total likely £400k minimum
findings.quote: The building is Grade II listed, has been vacant for an extended period and is now in disrepair. It requires significant restoration work before it can be brought back into educational use... No works should proceed unless and until officers have confirmed the full property, planning and heritage position and secured any necessary permissions or consents.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block funding is explicitly described as facing financial challenges where demand continues to exceed funding levels.
findings.detail: The paper names a structural funding gap in the Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block, where growth in SEND pupil numbers continues to outstrip available funding. This is a known national issue, but Sandwell explicitly identifies it as a constraint on its SEND strategy.
findings.matters: The DSG High Needs Block is a major education revenue stream. If demand is growing faster than funding, the council faces structural revenue budget pressure on education services. This is a named, specific challenge the council is flagging, not a hypothetical.
findings.figures: DSG High Needs block - 2026/27 allocation £6.5m; underlying demand gap not quantified
findings.quote: The Strategy is further aligned to the financial challenges within the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) High Needs Block, where demand for SEND provision continues to increase and exceed funding levels.

findings.headline: EHCP numbers forecast to rise from 5,156 to c.11,000 by 2030/31 if demand unmanaged.
findings.detail: Sandwell faces significant growth in demand for specialist education provision. The council currently has insufficient local places and is increasingly relying on expensive independent non-maintained special schools (INMSS) to place pupils. The paper explicitly states this creates 'pressures' that the capital programme aims to manage.
findings.matters: Growing service demand that outpaces local capacity creates revenue budget pressure, particularly if the authority continues paying premium rates for independent sector placements. A lender needs to understand whether these capital investments will actually reduce that expenditure or merely slow further deterioration.
findings.figures: 5,156 maintained EHCPs (June 2025); c.11,000 forecast by 2030/31
findings.quote: As of June 2025, the number of maintained EHCPs was 5,156. By 2030/31 Sandwell is forecast to have c11,000 pupils who will have an EHCP if this demand is unmanaged.

findings.headline: Council received £2.8m in dividend income from Birmingham Airport shares but does not budget for it, appropriately reserving it as uncertain and variable.
findings.detail: The council received £2.8m in dividends during the year. In line with treasury policy, this income is not included in operational budget plans due to the uncertainty of timing and amounts. The full dividend has been transferred to the Capital Financing earmarked reserve rather than used to offset debt costs.
findings.matters: One-off income can mask underlying budget performance if not properly separated. A lender needs to understand that underlying revenue pressures are not being relieved by this variable income, and that airport dividend support cannot be relied upon.
findings.figures: £2.8m dividend received; transferred entirely to Capital Financing earmarked reserve
findings.quote: Approximately £2.8m has been received in dividends from Birmingham Airport shares. In line with the strategy, the Council does not budget for this income due to the uncertainty of amounts and dates of receipt and therefore this amount will be transferred to the Capital Financing earmarked reserve.

findings.headline: Investment portfolio yields are declining despite outperforming the SONIA benchmark, with average annual yield falling from 4.28% in Q2 to 3.77% by end of year.
findings.detail: The council achieved investment returns of 4.10% average for the year, marginally above the SONIA benchmark of 4.01%, but the trend is sharply downward: Q1 5.29%, Q2 4.28%, Q3 4.07%, Q4 3.77%. This reflects general market conditions but reduces the financial flexibility that investment income provides as monetary policy eases.
findings.matters: Declining yields reduce cash generation from reserves and may force the council to either increase borrowing or reduce service spending if budget assumptions assumed higher treasury income. A lender needs to understand that treasury income support is diminishing.
findings.figures: Q1 2025/26 yield 5.29%; Q4 2025/26 yield 3.77%; Annual average 4.10%; SONIA benchmark 4.01%; Investment balances average £80m
findings.quote: whilst cash balances invested are similar compared to the previous year, the yield being achieved is seeing a reducing trend reflecting the current market

findings.headline: Council is explicitly pursuing a short-dated debt strategy, taking 1-5 year loans at current rates of 4.1-5.3%, with £93.2m (20% of total fixed-rate debt) due to mature within 12 months.
findings.detail: Rather than locking in rates for longer periods, the council has stated it will continue taking only short-dated debt due to market conditions, planning to refinance these loans to longer maturities when conditions improve. This creates material refinancing risk if interest rates do not fall as assumed. Recent new borrowing includes local authority loans at 4.55%, 4.90%, and 5.30%.
findings.matters: This is an active tactical bet on interest rates falling. If rates remain at 4-5% or higher when these loans mature, the council faces either paying materially higher refinancing costs or breaching its 6% net budget cap on borrowing costs. A lender needs to understand whether the council's budget plans have sufficient headroom for this scenario.
findings.figures: £93.241m (20.4% of total fixed-rate debt) due within 1 year; Q4 new borrowing rates: 4.30%, 4.33%, 4.55%, 4.73%, 4.90%, 5.00%, 5.30%
findings.quote: The current strategy will remain to only take short-dated debt (up to 5 years), due to market conditions, and to refinance for longer periods at the appropriate time to prevent a longer term cost burden on the council's revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Total external debt increased to £486.4m and £120m of new borrowing was taken in the year against an approved requirement of £118m.
findings.detail: The council's total debt portfolio grew by £44.7m (10%) from £441.7m to £486.4m. New fixed-term borrowing of £80m was taken in Q4 alone to support the capital programme, fund maturing loans, and maintain adequate cash balances. The £120m total new borrowing in the year slightly exceeded the approved £118m budget.
findings.matters: Material increase in council leverage means lenders need to understand whether the debt trajectory aligns with capital plans and revenue-generating capacity. Growing debt load increases the council's vulnerability to higher interest rates or economic shock.
findings.figures: Total debt 31 Mar 26: £486.364m (31 Mar 25: £441.696m); New borrowing: £120m vs approved £118m; Q4 borrowing alone: £80m
findings.quote: Debt balances have increased in the quarter as new fixed term borrowing of £80m has been taken to support the capital programme, to fund maturing loans, and also ensuring cash balances remain sufficient to service spending. This new borrowing is in accordance with the approved Treasury Management Strategy which indicated a total new borrowing requirement of £118m with actual new borrowing taken during the year of £120m.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £25.8m (29% of budget) into 2026/27, with major delays on Disabled Facilities Grant and regeneration
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme spent only £63.3m of £89.3m budget (71%), with £25.8m slipping into 2026/27. Major slippages include Disabled Facilities Grant (£6.678m of £11.639m, 57%), Economy & Regeneration schemes (£5.747m including Levelling Up Fund delays on Hydes Road Pavilion and Millennium Centre), and Property & Assets (£4.055m). The DFG programme shows the council has accumulated a multi-year balance and is planning to scale up delivery.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage indicates delivery challenges on major regeneration and infrastructure projects, which affects the council's ability to meet economic development targets and may signal cash flow or project management issues.
findings.figures: £25.8m total slippage, £6.678m DFG slippage, £5.747m Economy & Regeneration slippage, 71% delivery rate
findings.quote: Actual expenditure for the year totals £63.304m, representing 71% of the revised programme. This results in slippage of £25.810m into 2026/27 and later years

findings.headline: £3.532m of required efficiencies were not delivered in 2025/26, with £3.697m carried forward to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council delivered 83% of required efficiencies: 70% on an ongoing basis and 13% on a one-off basis. This left £3.532m of red-rated efficiencies undelivered. Of £6.343m total savings not delivered on an ongoing basis, £3.697m is carried forward to 2026/27, with the council also including £2.646m budget growth to remove the expectation of delivering some targets.
findings.matters: Consistent failure to deliver 17% of savings targets suggests structural budget management issues; future overspends are likely if these targets cannot be met in 2026/27.
findings.figures: £3.532m red-rated savings not delivered, £3.697m carried forward to 2026/27, 83% delivery rate, £2.646m budget growth added to remove expectations
findings.quote: 83% of the required efficiencies have been achieved. 70% have been rated as delivered on an ongoing basis (rated green), with 13% of efficiencies delivered on a one-off basis in year (rated blue)

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account £1.098m overspend masks £13.2m in underlying maintenance and repair cost pressures
findings.detail: The HRA recorded a managed £1.098m overspend, but underlying pressures totalled £13.2m: responsive asset management (£5.697m), void property works (£5.185m), and housing disrepair claims (£1.400m). These major costs were offset by capitalising £5.384m of works and achieving £4.075m in vacancy savings. The reserve fell from £51.150m to £50.052m.
findings.matters: The HRA is masking significant housing stock maintenance costs through capital accounting, reducing financial flexibility and indicating aging stock problems that will require sustained future investment.
findings.figures: £5.697m responsive works pressure, £5.185m void works pressure, £1.400m disrepair claims, £5.384m capitalised to offset
findings.quote: £5.697m budget pressure associated with responsive asset management works

findings.headline: Adult Social Care external placement costs overspent by £2.742m due to high-cost learning disability cases
findings.detail: Adult Social Care directorate overspent by £2.882m overall, with £2.742m specifically driven by external adult social care placement costs. The report notes that complex learning disability placements can cost in excess of £0.005m per week, meaning small increases in client numbers produce significant cost pressures.
findings.matters: Learning disability placement costs are typically structural and difficult to reduce; this signals ongoing budget pressure in adult social care that is unlikely to ease.
findings.figures: £2.742m overspend on external placements, £2.882m total Adult Social Care directorate overspend, £0.005m per week for complex learning disability placements
findings.quote: new high-cost learning disability placements, which are complex and can cost in excess of £0.005m per week, thus a significant increase in costs can result from a small growth in client numbers

findings.headline: Sandwell Children's Trust deficit remains at £18.2m despite £12.1m additional council funding in year
findings.detail: The council's wholly-owned children's social care provider was carrying a £19.8m deficit at end of 2024/25. Council approved £12.125m additional payments (£6.597m to address historic deficit, £5.528m for 2025/26 costs). However, SCT reported a £5.0m overspend at outturn, so the cumulative deficit fell only to £18.2m. The council now expects SCT to offset this £5.0m overspend over the next two years to stay on track for deficit clearance by end of 2027/28.
findings.matters: This is a material financial risk: a wholly-owned entity with a growing structural deficit despite large council injections, dependent on operational improvements that have not yet been demonstrated.
findings.figures: £18.2m cumulative deficit, £5.0m 2025/26 overspend, £12.125m total additional payments in 2025/26, £19.8m deficit at prior year-end
findings.quote: At outturn, the Trust has reported an overspend in 2025/26 of £5.0m, mainly due to further increased children's social care placement costs being incurred

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit of £6.053m replacing prior surplus, driven by SEND demand
findings.detail: The High Needs Block moved from a cumulative surplus of £2.696m to a deficit of £6.053m. This was driven by an in-year overspend of £8.749m caused by increased numbers of Education and Health Care Plans being issued and children being placed in higher-cost out-of-borough settings. findings.matters: This represents structural deficit spending in the highest-cost part of special education that will eventually hit the General Fund; the council is now creating contingency reserves to cover the residual cost in 2028.

findings.matters: One-off savings mask structural budget gaps that will reappear in future years. With a third of target efficiencies either uncertain or temporary, the council's underlying budget position may be weaker than headline figures suggest.

findings.matters: While reserves appear adequate, the level of overspend and the explicit MTFS warning that mitigations are essential suggest the HRA's current financial model is not sustainable without intervention.
findings.figures: £5.564m forecast overspend; HRA reserve: £51.150m (1 April 2025) reducing to £45.586m; £2.536m responsive maintenance pressure; £2.158m void works pressure; £1.4m disrepair claims

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.headline: Adult Social Care placement costs creating £2.088m directorate overspend, with high-cost learning disability cases as the primary driver
findings.detail: Adult Social Care and Health directorate is forecast to overspend by £2.088m. The main pressure is £1.510m on external adult social care placement costs, driven particularly by high-cost learning disability placements (individual placements costing in excess of £0.005m per week). Five new learning disability placements added during Q3 alone account for £0.750m of the pressure. Additional pressures include £0.891m from employee-related costs due to job evaluation outcomes and agency staff use.
findings.matters: Specialist placement costs are volatile and unpredictable. The council is seeing material cost growth from a small number of high-need cases, which creates both immediate budget risk and uncertainty over forward planning.
findings.figures: £2.088m overall directorate overspend; £1.510m placement cost pressure; £0.750m from 5 new learning disability placements added in Q3; individual placements can cost in excess of £0.005m per week

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block moving into £4.167m cumulative deficit despite government funding announcement
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is forecast to overspend by £6.863m in 2025/26. While the government announced in February 2026 it would fund 90% of such deficits through a 'high needs stability grant', only £3.750m is assumed eligible (subject to DfE approval of a local SEND reform plan), leaving the council with a residual £0.417m deficit.
findings.matters: The council faces a structural issue with education funding. Despite government support, it will carry a material deficit. The underlying cause—increased demand for SEND provision and insufficient local school places—shows no sign of resolution.

findings.detail: Sandwell Children's Trust accumulated a £19.8m deficit by end of 2024/25. findings.detail: Sandwell received additional £1.945m LNIP funding from CRSTS rebase in 2025/26, allocated specifically to road safety projects from local communities. findings.headline: CRSTS capital projects have required re-scoping due to construction inflation exceeding initial forecasts
findings.detail: Multiple projects within the £230.5m Sandwell CRSTS programme have been re-scoped since initial approval because construction inflation was higher than foreseen. This has compounded delays experienced in navigating WMCA governance and assurance framework approvals.

findings.paper_title: City Region Sustainable Transport Settlement Update and Local Transport Capital Programme 2026/27
findings.headline: Transport capital allocations declining in real-terms spending power despite nominal uplift from 2015 baseline
findings.detail: While LNIP allocations show a 21% uplift compared to 2015/16-2021/22 levels, when inflation is factored in, funding does not restore purchasing power to 2015 levels. With allocations fixed until 2026/27, the council faces year-on-year reduction in actual spending power for transport infrastructure maintenance and improvement.
findings.matters: Declining real-terms funding for essential highway maintenance signals potential sustainability issues in the council's infrastructure investment programme and may indicate future service or financial pressures

findings.headline: High Rise and Building Safety spending escalates to £9.45m in 2026/27 from £1.73m in 2025/26, representing a significant compliance cost increase
findings.detail: The High Rise and Building Safety budget increases from £1,729k in 2025/26 to £9,450k in 2026/27, a more than five-fold jump. This reflects increased activity in building safety compliance, with the 5-year programme showing a total increase of £1,013k. Spending continues at material levels: £6,989k, £7,091k, £7,192k, and £4,166k across the subsequent years, indicating a sustained multi-year commitment.
findings.matters: This represents a material and structural cost pressure on the council's capital resources that will compete with other investment priorities and affect debt servicing capacity over multiple years. Building safety compliance is a regulatory driver that reflects underlying housing stock condition issues.

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care costs escalating sharply from £24.2m (2026/27) to £69.0m (2030/31), driven by rising demand and complexity
findings.detail: Adult social care costs have risen 60% over the last five years. The MTFS forecast shows combined adult and children's social care growing from £24.239m in 2026/27 to £69.044m by 2030/31. This growth, driven by demographic demand and service complexity, increasingly dominates the council's financial trajectory. National Living Wage increases (from April 2026) add £0.633m of additional provider fees. The council is directing 'over £24m of budget growth into adult and children's social care in 2026/27' alone to protect services.
findings.matters: If social care costs escalate beyond the council's ability to find offsetting savings or demand management, future years become unaffordable. The steep trajectory suggests the transformation programme must succeed in productivity and prevention, not just efficiency.
findings.figures: Adult social care 5-year increase: 60%; 2026/27 social care growth: £24.239m; 2030/31 forecast: £69.044m; National Living Wage uplift from April 2026: £0.633m
findings.quote: In relation to adult social care, the cost to the council has increased by 60% over the last five years, driven by rising demand, increased complexity of needs and inflationary growth.

findings.headline: Forecast budget gaps in 2027/28 and 2028/29 despite three-year settlement, with funding growth of only £2.6m and £4.6m against net pressures of £69.5m and £89.1m
findings.detail: The three-year settlement provides certainty but minimal additional funding: £2.557m in 2027/28 and £4.625m in 2028/29. Against this, net pressures are forecast at £69.510m and £89.142m respectively, creating substantial gaps. The CFO explicitly acknowledges: 'There are forecast budget gaps in future years and therefore early engagement of options to meet that deficit will be vital'. The Reserves Strategy does not assume use of General Reserves to balance future years, placing reliance on transformation activity.
findings.matters: A lender examining sustainability needs sight of credible multi-year planning. Large unplanned gaps two years out, with the council explicitly requiring transformation at pace to close them, represents execution risk. The council must deliver proposals not yet detailed.
findings.figures: 2027/28: funding +£2.557m vs. pressures £69.510m (gap £66.953m); 2028/29: funding +£4.625m vs. pressures £89.142m (gap £84.517m)
findings.quote: There are forecast budget gaps in future years and therefore early engagement of options to meet that deficit will be vital to ensure that the ambitions of the Council Plan remain achievable.

findings.headline: Only 63% of 2025/26 efficiency targets achieved on an ongoing basis; £2.7m written off as unachievable
findings.detail: Of £21.070m efficiency targets required in 2025/26, only 63% (£13.378m) delivered on an ongoing basis, with 7% having plans for year-end delivery and 12% delivered one-off. The CFO has written £2.699m of unachievable targets into 2026/27 MTFP rather than carrying them forward, acknowledging these will not be delivered. This signals execution risk on future efficiency proposals.
findings.matters: If planned efficiencies consistently underdeliver, the council's ability to close future budget gaps becomes uncertain. The written-off £2.7m shows the council is adjusting, but £2.361m of new pressures also emerged mid-year from Q2 monitoring.
findings.figures: 2025/26 total efficiencies: £21.070m; delivered ongoing (green): £13.378m; unachievable being written out: £2.699m; Q2 emerging pressures: £2.361m added to MTFP
findings.quote: This has resulted in budget growth of £2.699m being added into the MTFP from 2026/27 in order to 'write out' the efficiency targets that are not considered deliverable.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account has shifted from balanced to in-deficit, dependent on financial mitigations to return to sustainability
findings.detail: The CFO reported in 2025 that the Housing Improvement Programme was balanced; now states this is no longer the case. The HRA is forecasting revenue deficits as it addresses backlogs of repairs, damp/mould, disrepair claims and void works in response to the Housing Regulator's C3 Assessment. Reserves have accumulated but the CFO notes this reflects 'delays in essential spending' rather than strategy. The MTFS identifies financial mitigations 'essential to ensure the HRA returns to a sustainable state', but these require close monitoring.
findings.matters: The HRA is ringfenced and funded separately from council tax. Deficits that depend on reserves or mitigations rather than operational sustainability create risk if mitigations underdeliver. The escalating backlog suggests the problem may worsen before improving.
findings.figures: 2025/26 budgeted HRA general reserve draw: £3.336m; current forecast draw: £6.493m (+£3.157m); drivers: backlog repairs, damp/mould, disrepair claims
findings.quote: I reported in 2025 that this programme was not unbalancing the HRA but the scale of the required response, alongside other relevant economic factors, means this is no longer the case. The revenue forecasts are in deficit as the Council addresses backlogs of work.

findings.headline: Sandwell Children's Trust (wholly owned subsidiary) has emerging accuracy issues in financial reporting and forecasting
findings.detail: The CFO identified emerging issues with the accuracy of financial reporting and forecasting within the Trust during and after contract negotiations. The Trust's £19m cumulative deficit was negotiated to zero in the three-year contract sum, but the reporting concerns require separate review of risks and resilience, supported by recent audits and Trust Board reviews. This is material given the Trust handles children's social care, a £24m+ budget area.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in a council's ability to forecast and control material commitments. Accuracy concerns in a wholly-owned services provider—particularly social care—create planning and cash flow risk if reporting proves unreliable.

I will review the risks and resilience of our current arrangements supported by recent audits and the internal reviews that are being considered by the Trust Board.

findings.paper_title: Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2026-2027 and Council Tax Resolution 2026-2027
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account requires £8.857m draw from general reserves to fund 2026-27 operations
findings.detail: While Sandwell's General Fund is balanced without requiring general reserves, the HRA cannot fund its 2026-27 operations from income alone and requires a contribution from HRA general reserves. This ongoing depletion of HRA reserves signals operational sustainability challenges in the housing business. The council is simultaneously running an £88.774m capital programme for HRA investment, creating tension between limited reserves and capital ambitions.
findings.matters: An HRA requiring annual reserve draws indicates the housing business cannot sustain itself from operational income. For lenders, this signals credit stress; reserves are the buffer against unexpected costs, service failures, or income shocks. Depleting reserves annually erodes financial resilience and constrains investment capacity.
findings.figures: £8.857m draw from HRA reserves in 2026/27; HRA capital programme £88.774m for 2026/27
findings.quote: including the draw of £8.857m from HRA reserves in 2026/27

findings.headline: Finance team capacity constraints and new ledger implementation placed significant operational pressure
findings.detail: The council implemented a new financial ledger system during the year, which placed significant pressure on the finance team and limited their ability to support audit planning and interim work in spring 2025. This contributed to the late accounts submission and the fact that accounts did not undergo expected internal quality review.
findings.matters: Finance function capacity constraints driven by system implementation increase the risk of continued delays and errors in future years, and may indicate need for additional resources or extended timelines.
findings.figures: Draft accounts received mid-August; interim work essential for timetable reset; aim to complete 2025/26 audit by end of November 2026
findings.quote: The delay needs to be viewed in the context of the new ledger implementation, which placed significant pressure on the finance team. Due to the time pressures, the accounts did not undergo the expected level of internal quality review.

findings.headline: Systematic mapping and accounting errors in high-needs and other income/expenditure streams
findings.detail: Testing identified multiple errors in how transactions were coded to the correct service lines. The High Needs Block showed a £14.819m overstatement of both income and expenditure that should have been netted off. Design team fees were misstated by £1.2m, and schools catering expenditure by £5.317m due to incorrect accounting for costs.
findings.matters: Systematic errors across multiple income streams indicate weaknesses in the finance function's ability to accurately classify and record transactions, suggesting the accounts require extensive manual adjustments and remain error-prone.
findings.figures: High Needs Block £14.819m; Design team fees £1.2m; Schools catering £5.317m; Total audit adjustments £12.3m
findings.quote: High Needs Block: Two related sample errors resulted in a £14,819k overstatement of both income and expenditure. These amounts should have been netted off. Design team fees: Income and expenditure were overstated by £1.2m due to incorrect accounting for design team salary costs relating to capital projects.

findings.headline: Draft accounts published 6 weeks late after statutory deadline, audit started late affecting review of high-risk areas
findings.detail: Draft accounts were not delivered until mid-August, 6 weeks later than planned and after the 30 June statutory publication deadline. This late start meant key areas such as property valuations—historically challenging—were considered later in the audit process.
findings.matters: Late accounts delivery indicates governance and finance function challenges, and delays the audit process, leaving less time to complete work before statutory deadlines and increasing risk of disclaimed opinions.
findings.figures: Accounts due 30 June 2025; draft accounts received mid-August 2025; backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We did not receive the draft accounts until mid-August. This was after the statutory publication deadline of 30 June and six weeks later than the date management had agreed for us to start the audit. The delay needs to be viewed in the context of the new ledger implementation, which placed significant pressure on the finance team.

findings.headline: Goods received not invoiced accrual process failure creates £8.4m potential overstatement of liabilities
findings.detail: Testing identified that £9m of the £27.223m GRNI balance related to items that should have been cancelled, including provisional purchase orders and goods-received notes against cancelled orders. When management tested the proposed £9m adjustment, only £0.673m could be validated. The £8.4m difference represents a potential overstatement of liabilities.
findings.matters: Control failures in the accrual process mean the council's financial statements may overstate liabilities by £8.4m, creating uncertainty about the true position of payables and reserves.
findings.figures: £27.223m total GRNI balance; £9m items that should have been cancelled; £0.673m validated adjustment; £8.4m unvalidated
findings.quote: Of the £27.223m GRNI balance, £9m related to items that should have been cancelled. These included provisional purchase orders, retrospective PO creation, and goods-received notes raised against cancelled or disputed orders. As a result, the GRNI accrual was inaccurate. Our testing has confirmed only £0.673m of this proposed adjustment. Management has therefore decided not to amend the 2024/25 accounts. This leaves a potential £8.4m overstatement of liabilities in the 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.headline: Disabled audit logs and excessive system access created significant control weakness over journal posting
findings.detail: Audit testing found that audit logs—essential controls for monitoring unauthorised transactions—were not enabled in the Oracle EBS system. Additionally, too many staff had enhanced system access rights, increasing the risk that inappropriate or unauthorised journals could be posted without detection.
findings.matters: Disabled audit logging combined with excessive access rights is a fundamental control weakness that increases fraud risk and undermines the reliability of financial reporting controls.
findings.figures: Extended journal testing performed; journals could be posted without approval for the first six months of the year
findings.quote: We noted that too many staff had enhanced system access rights, which increases the risk that inappropriate or unauthorised journals could be posted without detection. We also found that audit logs—an important control for monitoring system activity—were not enabled. The absence of audit logging is a significant control weakness.

findings.headline: Children's Trust entity carries £19m cumulative overspend in reserves
findings.detail: The council's group entity, the Children's Trust, had a cumulative deficit of £19m in its reserves at 31 March 2025. The auditor initially questioned whether group accounts were required based on materiality, but the £19m deficit demonstrates this is a material group liability.
findings.matters: A £19m overspend in a key council service (children's services) that is being consolidated into the group accounts is a material liability affecting the council's overall financial position and sustainability.
findings.figures: £19m cumulative overspend in Children's Trust reserves at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Children's Trust had a cumulative £19m overspend in its reserves at 31 March 2025. This meant the CT accounts did include material balances, and we did not agree with management's conclusion that group accounts were not required on the basis of materiality.

findings.headline: Auditor unable to form opinion on financial statements due to lack of evidence on opening balances
findings.detail: The auditor has issued a disclaimed opinion for the second consecutive year, unable to obtain sufficient evidence to support an unmodified audit opinion before the 27 February 2026 backstop date. Without assurance over opening balances carried forward from the prior year's disclaimed opinion, the auditor cannot form an opinion on the financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the council's accounts lack independent verification and raises fundamental questions about the reliability of its financial position for anyone assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026; accounts for year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: Because previous years' audits received backstop-related disclaimed opinions, we have been unable to obtain enough evidence to support an unmodified audit opinion before the backstop date of 27 February 2026. Without assurance over the opening balances, we cannot form an opinion on the financial statements.
